So 'Creates a GPIO interface ...'. 'Implements necessary ...'

See my comments in the constructor. I think we should not have a pretend starting "de-glitched" value for the GPIO. We should not successfully return a value until we've read the GPIO enough times to be valid.

You could change the return type of the get method to be std::optional<int>. Then the method could return undefined if:
* This is the first read, so we have no previous read to compare against.
* We have not seen two reads in a row that matched, so we still don't know what the value is.

For initial startup, another option would be to do N reads in a row, perhaps with a very short sleep in between. That would give you a previous reading or two right away. However, if they don't agree it is still unclear what to return. It could throw an exception I suppose, since that is an error situation.
Done

What is the goal of this flag throughout this commit?
* To allow for early testing of JSON config files on very early hardware/simulation before all the GPIOs have been set up in the kernel?
* To allow for automated testing?

The solution for the two is very different I think.

## Suggestions if trying to allow for early testing

Hardcoding this in the C++ class seems like it won't work for upstream code. One user of the application might want to have it false, and another might want it to be true.

You could make it a command line parameter or a build flag.

However, a simpler approach might be to do the following:
* Don't create the gpiod::line object in the constructor. This allows the constructor to succeed and the Gpio object to exist.
* Create the gpiod::line object if needed when one of the Gpio request methods is called. Throw an exception then if the find_line() fails.
* Let the caller of the Gpio request method decide how to handle the exception. They could choose to retry a few times and then log an error message.

This would eliminate the need for all the JSON parser changes.

## Suggestions if trying to allow for automated testing

In this case, I'd suggest using the standard approach of:
* Abstract base GPIO class
* Concrete sub-class that does the real thing
* Mock sub-class for automated tests

You already have the first two, and creating the mock class is very simple. Then you just have to decide how to cause the real subclass to be created for production usage and the mock subclass to be created for automated tests.

Two approaches used in this repository:
* Create a Services hierarchy with the same three classes (ABC/real/mock). Add a createGPIO method to the Services class. The real subclass creates a real GPIO, and the mock subclass creates a mock GPIO. This Services hierarchy can handle other real/mock problems in the future too, such as error logging and getting data from D-Bus.
* Create a global scope createGPIO function in the GPIO header file. Provide two implementations in two different .C files. Then link in the implementation that produces a real GPIO when linking the real application. Link in the implementation that produces a mock GPIO when linking the test cases.
Done

Nit: It is recommended to use the pre-increment operator (++requestFailureCount) rather that the post-increment operator unless you really need to post-increment behavior.

For simple types like int there is probably no difference. But for classes that support pre/post, the post variation may require the class to create and return a temporary copy.
